claims.text: Premelting and melting in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are governed by local compositional fluctuations.
Local compositional fluctuations create a distribution of atomic bond energies.
The phase transition is gradual and begins at the nanoparticle surface.
Regions with lower cohesive energy premelt at lower temperatures.
The nanoparticle core remains solid until temperatures higher than those causing surface premelting.
The nanoparticles are initially solid and equiatomic in Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
The synthesis produces a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Temperature-resolved in situ structural observation and calorimetry can compare the premelting and melting response of the HEA with baseline nanoparticles.
Spatial composition variations and local short-range order produce spatially varying cohesive and surface energies.
Differences among constituent atomic radii and bonding characteristics create regions with lower effective cohesive energy, particularly at the surface.
Low-effective-cohesive-energy surface regions cause progressive, spatially inhomogeneous premelting followed by delayed core melting.
Chemical complexity broadens the melting transition relative to simpler metallic nanoparticles.
The HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a premelted surface layer over a wider temperature interval than the baseline particles.
The onset of complete melting will be delayed in the HEA nanoparticles relative to the baseline particles.
Single-metal or binary-alloy nanoparticle baselines typically have more homogeneous and sharper melting transitions.
The proposed mechanism applies in the 10–100 nm size range, where surface effects are expected to dominate.
Phase segregation may produce behavior different from that predicted for a single-phase solid solution.
A melting transition as sharp as or sharper than that of the baseline would falsify the proposed local-fluctuation-mediated broadening mechanism.
